newsitem.title: USA: White House decides against Internet taxes.
newsitem.headline: White House decides against Internet taxes.

text.p: The Clinton administration, after a two-year study, has decided not to call for new taxes or regulations on business conducted over the Internet, The Washington Post reported in Monday editions.
In a report to be released on Monday by President Bill Clinton, the administration will endorse letting the private sector largely determine how it will operate in cyberspace, the newspaper said.

In the final draft of the report, the U.S. government argues for a non-regulatory, market-oriented approach in order not to hamper development of business on the Internet, which it estimates could total "tens of billions of dollars by the turn of the century."
The report will likely please industry leaders, who have argued that new laws and taxes could dampen development of electronic commerce.

The administration's decision not to impose taxes or regulations on commerce on the global computer network follows last week's decision by the Supreme Court to strike down a law restricting indecent speech online.

Although the administration had supported the law, it is now asking the industry to instead police itself through a ratings system and advocating the use of software that lets parents block children's access to objectionable Internet content.

"Unnecessary regulation could cripple the growth and diversity of the Internet," the Post quoted the report as saying. "The administration therefore supports industry self-regulation, adoption of competing ratings systems and development of easy-to-use technical solutions...to assist in screening information online."
The report advocates that other governments adopt a similar approach toward taxes and content regulations in an effort to ease electronic transactions across national borders.
Within the United States, sales taxes, levied by states, would still apply to good purchased on the Internet.

After unveiling the report, Clinton is expected to issue a series of challenges to federal agencies, Congress and the private sector to implement specific recommendations, the Post quoted a senior administration official as saying.
Clinton would also set up a commission, to be chaired by Vice President Al Gore, that would oversee the effort and ensure its completion by Jan. 1, 2000, it said.

The report calls for giving companies and advocacy groups a chance to devise technologies and practices to control the collection of information such as names, addresses and telephone numbers from children. If the issue is not given prompt attention the document urges government action, according to the newspaper report.
The report urged continued government controls on the export of software with strong encryption technology.
